questions.question: What does the continuum hypothesis assert?
options: Every infinite set has cardinality $\aleph_0$ or $\mathfrak{c}$.
No cardinality lies strictly between $\aleph_0$ and $\mathfrak{c}$.
No set has cardinality strictly larger than $\mathfrak{c}$.

questions.question: Which two cardinalities are compared in the continuum hypothesis?
options: $\mathbb{N}$ and $\mathbb{Z}$ as labelled sets rather than cardinalities

questions.question: What kind of set would refute the continuum hypothesis?
What is the informal question behind the continuum hypothesis?
options: Is there an intermediate infinity between $\mathbb{N}$ and $\mathbb{R}$?
Are there real numbers between two distinct integers?
Can every matrix be diagonalised over $\mathbb{R}$?
Does every finite set have a power set?

questions.question: Does the continuum hypothesis claim that $\mathbb{R}$ is countable?
options: No. It asks if a cardinality lies between $\aleph_0$ and $\mathfrak{c}$.
Yes. It says no infinite cardinality lies above $\aleph_0$.
No. It says $\mathbb{R}$ has no subsets of size $\aleph_0$.

questions.question: Which cardinality condition is ruled out if the continuum hypothesis is assumed true?
Assume the continuum hypothesis. Can there be a set $A$ with $\aleph_0 \lt \operatorname{card}(A) \lt \mathfrak{c}$?
options: Yes, because the hypothesis only concerns subsets of $\mathbb{R}$
Yes, since Cantor's theorem gives sets of every cardinality
No, because the hypothesis rules out such a cardinality
No, because every uncountable set has cardinality $\mathfrak{c}$

questions.question: Assume the continuum hypothesis. If $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable, what cardinality must $A$ have?
Does a countably infinite set violate the continuum hypothesis?
options: Yes. It is strictly smaller than $\mathfrak{c}$, which is enough.
Yes. Its size $\aleph_0$ lies between $\aleph_0$ and $\mathfrak{c}$.
No. Its cardinality is exactly $\aleph_0$, an endpoint.
No. Its cardinality is $\mathfrak{c}$, the upper endpoint.

questions.question: Does a set of cardinality $\mathfrak{c}$ violate the continuum hypothesis?
options: Yes. Every uncountable set violates the continuum hypothesis.
Yes. $\mathfrak{c}$ is strictly above $\aleph_0$, which is enough.
No. $\mathfrak{c}$ is the upper endpoint, not strictly between.
No. The hypothesis only concerns sets smaller than $\aleph_0$.

questions.question: Why do $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}$ not by themselves settle the continuum hypothesis?
options: $\mathbb{Q}$ is $\aleph_0$ and $\mathbb{R}$ is $\mathfrak{c}$, so they only show the endpoints.
$\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}$ both have cardinality $\mathfrak{c}$, so no gap can appear.
The hypothesis concerns subsets of $\mathbb{N}$, not $\mathbb{Q}$ or $\mathbb{R}$.

questions.question: What is the negation of the continuum hypothesis?
What does the strictness in $\aleph_0 \lt \operatorname{card}(A) \lt \mathfrak{c}$ exclude?
Assume the continuum hypothesis. If $A$ is infinite and $\operatorname{card}(A) \lt \mathfrak{c}$, what must be true about $A$?
Which set is not an intermediate-size counterexample to the continuum hypothesis?
options: A subset of $\mathbb{R}$ whose cardinality is strictly greater than $\aleph_0$ and strictly less than $\mathfrak{c}$
A hypothetical set of cardinality strictly between countable infinity and the continuum

questions.question: If $\operatorname{card}(A)=2^{\aleph_0}$, what is $\operatorname{card}(A)$ in continuum notation?
Why does Cantor's theorem alone not answer the continuum hypothesis?
options: It gives only $\aleph_0\le\mathfrak{c}$, not a strict inequality between them.
It shows $\aleph_0 \lt \mathfrak{c}$, not whether a cardinality lies between.
It shows that $2^{\mathfrak{c}}$ lies strictly between $\aleph_0$ and $\mathfrak{c}$.
It applies only to finite sets, not to infinite sets such as $\mathbb{N}$.

questions.question: Assume the continuum hypothesis. What are the possible cardinalities of a subset $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$?
Which statement would be a direct counterexample to the continuum hypothesis?
Assume the continuum hypothesis. If $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ is neither finite nor countable, what must be true?
options: $A$ must have cardinality strictly between $\aleph_0$ and $\mathfrak{c}$
